o: Who did phone you last night?
Who did you phoned last night?
R1.e: When 'who' is the subject of the question, we don't use do/did: Who phoned you?

R1.q: The path was so treacherous after the storm that two walkers slipped and fell. Treacherous means...
R1.e: The context helps: people slipped and fell, so the path was dangerous.

R1.q: I don't eat meat. — ___ I. I'm a vegetarian too.
R1.e: To agree with a negative sentence we use Neither + auxiliary + I. The auxiliary here is 'do'.

R1.q: The ___ (long) you wait, the harder it gets.
R1.e: The + comparative..., the + comparative: the longer..., the harder...

R1.q: My cousin is very ___-working: she studies every evening.
R1.e: Hard-working is a compound adjective for someone who works a lot.

R1.q: Sorry I'm late. How long ___ here?
R1.e: We use the present perfect continuous with 'how long' for an action that started in the past and is still happening.

R1.q: We ___ (know) each other since primary school.
R1.e: 'Know' is a state verb, so we use the present perfect simple, not the continuous, with 'since'.

R1.q: He was stung by a ___ in the garden and his arm swelled up.
R1.e: A wasp is an insect that can sting you. A rash, blister or bruise is something on your skin, not something that stings.
Adjective order: opinion (lovely), size (long), colour (red), material (woollen).

R1.q: The opposite of 'loose' clothes is t___ clothes.
R1.e: Tight clothes are small and close to your body; loose clothes are big and comfortable.

R1.q: By the time we reached the airport, we ___ for over two hours in traffic.
R1.e: Past perfect continuous: an action that continued up to a moment in the past (by the time we reached...).

R1.q: The queue was ___ long that we nearly missed our flight.
R1.e: We use so + adjective + that. We use such + (a) + adjective + noun + that.

R1.q: You have to go through ___, where they check your hand luggage, before the departure lounge.
R1.e: At security they check you and your hand luggage before you go to the departure lounge.
Adverbs of manner usually go after the verb and its object, not between them: speaks English very well.

R1.q: I didn't feel like going to the party, but I went a___.
R1.e: Anyway means 'although there was a reason not to'. It usually goes at the end of the sentence.

R2.q: At midday tomorrow I ___ over the Alps on my way to London.
R2.e: Future continuous: an action in progress at a specific time in the future (at midday tomorrow).

R2.q: By the time you arrive, the film ___ (start).
R2.e: Future perfect: an action that will be finished before a time in the future (by the time you arrive).

R2.q: During the storm, a tree was hit by ___.
R2.e: Lightning is the flash of light in a storm; it can hit trees. Thunder is only the noise. Lighting means lamps and lights.

R2.q: We should r___ plastic bottles instead of throwing them away.
R2.e: To recycle is to make something new from old material. To reuse is to use something again.

R2.q: If you mix blue and yellow, you ___ green.
R2.e: Zero conditional for things that are always true: if + present, present.

R2.q: I'll lend you my notes as long as you ___ them back tomorrow.
R2.e: After when, until, as long as and unless with a future meaning, we use the present simple, not will.

R2.q: We'll have lunch when Dad ___ (get) home.
R2.e: After 'when' talking about the future, we use the present simple: when Dad gets home.

R2.q: We should take ___ of the good weather and go to the beach.
R2.e: Take advantage of something = use a good situation. The other nouns don't go with 'take ... of'.

R2.q: If she ___ the alarm, she wouldn't have been late.
R2.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. It's about an imaginary past.

R2.q: I'd tell you the answer if I ___ it.
R2.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb. It's about an imaginary present.

R2.q: Before my driving test I was so ___ that my hands were shaking.
R2.e: When you're nervous, you're worried about something that is going to happen, and your hands may shake.
Furious is a strong adjective meaning extremely angry.

R2.q: I wish it ___ raining. I want to go out!
R2.e: Wish + would for something we want to change in the present or future, often because it annoys us.

R2.q: I wish I ___ (not say) that to her yesterday.
R2.e: Wish + past perfect for regrets about the past.

R2.q: The long queue at the post office was really ___.
R2.e: -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes the feeling (the queue). -ed adjectives describe how a person feels.

R3.q: When we were kids, my sister and I ___ fight all the time.
R3.e: We can use would + verb for repeated actions in the past, like 'used to'.

R3.q: I can't get used to ___ (work) at night.
R3.e: After get used to / be used to we use the -ing form, because 'to' is a preposition here.

R3.q: I was so tired that I fell ___ on the sofa during the film.
R3.e: Fall asleep = start sleeping. We say 'fall asleep', not 'fall sleep'.

R3.q: Remember ___ the lights before you leave.
R3.e: Remember + to + infinitive = don't forget to do something in the future.

R3.q: The singer's new ___ has twelve songs on it.
R3.e: An album is a collection of songs released together.

R3.q: The ground is wet. It ___ rained last night.
R3.e: Must have + past participle: we're sure something happened in the past because of the evidence.

R3.q: I'd rather ___ (walk) than take the bus.
R3.e: I'd rather + infinitive without 'to' when talking about our own preference.

R3.q: I'm ___ for the bus. It's late again!
R3.e: Wait for = stay somewhere until something comes. Expect doesn't take 'for' and means to think something will happen.

R3.q: This soup ___ a bit strange. Is it still OK?
R3.e: Verbs of the senses + adjective: tastes strange. We use 'like' before a noun, not an adjective.

R3.q: She ___ her shoulders to show she didn't know the answer.
R3.e: When you shrug your shoulders, you lift them up to show you don't know or don't care.

R3.q: The part of your leg that bends in the middle: k___
R3.e: Your knee is the joint in the middle of your leg.

R3.q: Someone who steals from shops is a ___.
R3.e: A shoplifter takes things from shops without paying. A burglar breaks into houses.

R3.q: We're having our kitchen ___ (paint) next week.
R3.e: Have + object + past participle: someone else does the job for us.

R3.q: He ___ me that the shop was closed.
R3.e: Warn + person + that... Suggest, explain and say don't take a person directly after them.

R3.q: The person who reads the news on TV or radio: a n___
R3.e: A newsreader (or newscaster) presents the news on TV or radio.

R4.q: ___ it was very expensive, they bought the car.
R4.e: Although + subject + verb. Despite and in spite of are followed by a noun or -ing form.

R4.q: I left early ___ miss the traffic.
R4.e: So as not to / in order not to + infinitive for a negative purpose.

R4.q: She wore a coat so ___ she wouldn't get cold.
R4.e: So that + subject + verb expresses purpose, often with would/could.

R4.q: The company is doing badly and might go ___.
R4.e: Go bankrupt = have no money to pay debts, so the business must close.

R4.q: An advert on TV or radio: a c___
R4.e: A commercial is an advertisement on TV or radio.

R4.q: The police ___ looking for a young man in a red jacket.
R4.e: 'Police' is a plural noun, so it takes a plural verb: the police are.
Homework is uncountable, so we can't use many, a few or several with it.
The prefix dis- makes the opposite of some adjectives: honest - dishonest.

R4.q: Which word means 'to cook too much'?
R4.e: The prefix over- means 'too much'. Under- means 'not enough'.

R4.q: ___ of the two answers is correct; they're both wrong.
R4.e: Neither = not one and not the other (of two). We use 'none' for more than two.

R4.q: E___ student in the class got a certificate.
R4.e: Every / each + singular noun: every student, each student.

R4.q: The results of the experiment ___ the theory.
R4.e: To prove a theory = to show that it's true.

R4.q: We usually have ___ lunch at two o'clock.
R4.e: We don't use an article with meals in general: have lunch, have breakfast.

R4.q: I'm sick and t___ of this rain!
R4.e: Sick and tired is a word pair meaning very bored or annoyed with something.

R4.q: The show was a bit hit and ___: some songs were great, others were terrible.
R4.e: Hit and miss is a word pair meaning sometimes good and sometimes bad.

T1.q: Which question is correct?
o: What did happen at the meeting?
What did happened at the meeting?
What was happen at the meeting?
T1.e: 'What' is the subject here, so we don't use did: What happened?

T1.q: Do you know what time ___?
T1.e: In indirect questions (Do you know...?) we use normal word order: subject + verb.

T1.q: Who ___ this song? It's great!
T1.e: 'Who' is the subject of the question, so we use the normal past simple: Who wrote...?

T1.q: What ___ (you / think) of the film last night?
T1.e: In past simple questions we use did + subject + infinitive: What did you think?

T1.q: After the hike we were parched, so we drank three bottles of water. Parched means...
T1.e: They drank lots of water, so parched must mean very thirsty.

T1.q: The old man was so feeble that he needed help to stand up. Feeble means...
T1.e: He needed help to stand up, so feeble must mean weak.

T1.q: You haven't seen my glasses, ___?
T1.e: Negative sentence + positive question tag, with the same auxiliary: haven't... have you?

T1.q: A: I didn't like the film. B: Didn't you? I ___! I thought it was brilliant.
T1.e: To say you're different, use the opposite auxiliary: I didn't like it. - I did!

T1.q: The ___ (hot) it gets, the more water you need to drink.
T1.e: The + comparative..., the + comparative: the hotter..., the more...

T1.q: Someone who is ___-minded is happy to listen to new ideas.
T1.e: Open-minded = willing to accept new ideas. Absent-minded means forgetful.

T1.q: The final question was ___ impossible - nobody got it right.
T1.e: With extreme adjectives like impossible, we use absolutely, not very or fairly.

T1.q: Someone who is very kind and friendly is w___-hearted.
T1.e: Warm-hearted is a compound adjective for a kind, friendly person.

T1.q: This jacket doesn't ___ your trousers; the colours are completely different.
T1.e: Match = look good together. Fit is about the right size.

T1.q: Your hands are dirty! What ___?
T1.e: Present perfect continuous to ask about a recent activity that explains a present result.

T1.q: She ___ (not feel) well since Monday.
T1.e: Present perfect (simple or continuous) with 'since' for a situation that started in the past and continues now.

T1.q: I've got a ___ nose and I keep sneezing.
T1.e: A runny nose is a common symptom of a cold.

T1.q: The cut was deep, so the doctor gave me ___.
T1.e: Stitches close a deep cut. A doctor can't 'give' you a rash or hiccups to help you.

T1.q: ___ unemployed need more support from the government.
T1.e: The + adjective can mean a group of people: the unemployed, the rich, the young.

T1.q: He bought ___ (leather / black / expensive) boots.
T1.e: Adjective order: opinion (expensive), colour (black), material (leather).

T1.q: Clothes that are big and loose, not tight, are b___.
T1.e: Baggy clothes are very loose on your body.

T2.q: When I got to the check-in desk, I realised I ___ my passport at home.
T2.e: Past perfect: an action that happened before another past action (I realised).

T2.q: We ___ along the beach when it started to rain.
T2.e: Past continuous for an action in progress when another action interrupted it.

T2.q: She was tired because she ___ all night.
T2.e: Past perfect continuous: a long activity before a past moment that explains a past result.

T2.q: It was ___ bad weather that all flights were cancelled.
T2.e: Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather). We don't use 'a' with uncountable nouns.

T2.q: The seats were ___ uncomfortable that I couldn't sleep.
T2.e: So + adjective + that. Too is not followed by 'that'.

T2.q: By the time the plane took off, we ___ (sit) on it for two hours.
T2.e: Past perfect continuous with 'for' for an action that continued up to a past moment.

T2.q: I ___ (never / fly) before my trip to London last year.
T2.e: Past perfect for experience before a time in the past. Fly - flew - flown.

T2.q: They were ___ friendly people that we felt at home immediately.
T2.e: Such + adjective + plural noun + that.

T2.q: The ___ is the person who flies the plane.
T2.e: The pilot flies the plane. The cabin crew and stewards look after passengers.

T2.q: Our flight was ___ because of fog, so we waited for six hours.
T2.e: A delayed flight leaves later than planned.

T2.q: Before your flight, you ___ at the desk and leave your big suitcase.
T2.e: At the airport you check in: you show your ticket and leave your big bags.

T2.q: A small bag you take with you onto the plane: hand l___
T2.e: Hand luggage is the bag you keep with you in the cabin.

T2.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I have breakfast always at seven.
I always have breakfast at seven.
I have always breakfast at seven.
Always I have breakfast at seven.
T2.e: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: I always have...

T2.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She probably's going to be late.
She's going to be probably late.
She's probably going to be late.
She's going probably to be late.
T2.e: Probably goes after the verb 'be' (she's probably), not in the middle of 'going to'.

T2.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: He plays the guitar quite badly.
He plays quite badly the guitar.
He quite badly plays the guitar.
Quite badly he plays the guitar.
T2.e: Adverbs of manner go after the verb + object: plays the guitar badly.

T2.q: I have seen that film. (already) = I have ___ that film.
T2.e: Already usually goes between the auxiliary (have) and the main verb.

T2.q: We'd hoped for sun, but ___ it rained all week.
T2.e: Unfortunately introduces bad news, which is different from what we hoped.

T2.q: I thought the test would be hard, but it was ___ quite easy.
T2.e: Actually = in fact. We use it when the truth is different from what we expected.

T2.q: We looked for our cat for days and ___ we found her in a neighbour's garage.
T2.e: Eventually = in the end, after a long time.

T2.q: I was so tired that I ___ (near) fell asleep in class.
T2.e: Nearly = almost. We make the adverb from 'near' + -ly.

T3.q: In ten years' time, I hope I ___ as a doctor.
T3.e: Future continuous for an action in progress at a time in the future.

T3.q: Hurry up! By the time we get there, the concert ___.
T3.e: Future perfect: the concert will be over before we arrive.

T3.q: This time next week, we ___ in the sea in Mondello.
T3.e: Future continuous with 'this time next week' for an action in progress then.

T3.q: By the end of the month, I ___ this book.
T3.e: By + future time + future perfect: the action will be complete.

T3.q: Can I call you at eight, or ___ (you / have) dinner then?
T3.e: Future continuous question for an action in progress at a future time (at eight). 'Are you having' is also possible.

T3.q: By the time you come back from holiday, I ___ (paint) the kitchen.
T3.e: Future perfect: will have + past participle for an action finished before a future time.

T3.q: It's not really raining, just a bit of ___.
T3.e: Drizzle is very light rain.

T3.q: The air in big cities is often full of ___ from cars.
T3.e: Pollution is dirty air, water or land caused by people and machines.

T3.q: It's freezing and there's ___ on the car windows this morning.
T3.e: Frost is a thin white layer of ice that forms when it's very cold.

T3.q: Weather that is hot and wet, where the air feels heavy: h___
T3.e: Humid weather is hot with a lot of water in the air.

T3.q: If you don't water plants, they ___.
T3.e: Zero conditional for general truths: if + present, present.

T3.q: I'll phone you ___ I get home.
T3.e: As soon as = immediately after. It's followed by the present when we talk about the future.

T3.q: You can't go to the party ___ you finish your homework first.
T3.e: Unless = if not: you can't go if you don't finish your homework.

T3.q: We'll stay at the beach until the sun ___.
T3.e: After until, when, as soon as (future meaning) we use the present simple.

T3.q: Unless it ___ (stop) raining soon, the match will be cancelled.
T3.e: Unless + present simple in first conditional sentences.

T3.q: When you choose a school, you must take the cost into ___.
T3.e: Take something into account = think about it when you decide.

T3.q: Could you take ___ my plants while I'm on holiday?
T3.e: Take care of = look after. Take after means to look or behave like an older relative.

T3.q: Don't take it ___ - she wasn't criticising you.
T3.e: Take something personally = feel that a comment is an attack on you.

T3.q: My dad took ___ the family business when my grandfather retired.
T3.e: Take over = start being responsible for something from someone else.

T3.q: When the plane leaves the ground, it takes o___.
T3.e: Take off = when a plane leaves the ground and starts flying.

T4.q: If I ___ more free time, I'd learn to play the guitar.
T4.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb for an imaginary present situation.

T4.q: If you'd told me about the problem, I ___ you.
T4.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

T4.q: What ___ if you saw a ghost?
T4.e: Second conditional question: What would you do if + past simple?

T4.q: If she hadn't missed the bus, she ___ late for work.
T4.e: Third conditional: the result in the past is would (not) have + past participle.

T4.q: If I ___ (be) taller, I'd play basketball.
T4.e: In the second conditional we can use were or was after I/he/she/it.

T4.q: We ___ (not get) lost if we'd taken a map.
T4.e: Third conditional result: wouldn't have + past participle.

T4.q: I'm really ___ about the school trip tomorrow! I can't wait!
T4.e: Excited = very happy about something that is going to happen.

T4.q: He was ___ when he couldn't find his little son in the crowd.
T4.e: Terrified = extremely frightened.

T4.q: When the police found the lost dog, the owners felt very ___.
T4.e: Relieved = happy because something bad has ended or didn't happen.

T4.q: Feeling bad because you've done something wrong: g___
T4.e: You feel guilty when you know you've done something wrong.

T4.q: I wish I ___ a car. The buses are terrible here.
T4.e: Wish + past simple for a present situation we want to be different.

T4.q: I wish I ___ that film. It was awful!
T4.e: Wish + past perfect for a regret about the past.

T4.q: I wish you ___ your phone at the dinner table. It's so rude!
T4.e: Wish + would for someone else's annoying habit that we want to change.

T4.q: If only I ___ harder last year - I'd have a better job now.
T4.e: If only + past perfect for a past regret, like 'I wish'.

T4.q: I wish I ___ (live) closer to the sea.
T4.e: Wish + past simple for a present situation that we'd like to be different.

T4.q: I wish my brother ___ (stop) borrowing my things without asking!
T4.e: Wish + would for something annoying that we want someone to change.

T4.q: The instructions were so ___ that I couldn't build the bookcase.
T4.e: -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes the feeling: the instructions were confusing.

T4.q: I was really ___ when I fell over in front of the whole class.
T4.e: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels: I was embarrassed.

T4.q: The noise from the building work ___ (annoy) me all day yesterday.
T4.e: Annoy is a verb that expresses a feeling. For yesterday we need a past form: annoyed (or was annoying).

T4.q: It really ___ me when people drop litter on the beach.
T4.e: Upset is a verb of feeling: it + upsets + me. We need the -s for 'it'.

T5.q: I ___ to get up at six, but now I start work at nine.
T5.e: Used to + infinitive for past habits that are not true now.

T5.q: After a few weeks in England, I ___ used to the food.
T5.e: Get used to = become familiar with something new.

T5.q: She's a nurse, so she's used to ___ (sleep) during the day.
T5.e: Be used to + -ing form = be familiar with something.

T5.q: I set my ___ for seven o'clock.
T5.e: You set an alarm (clock) to wake you up at a certain time.

T5.q: When you're tired, you open your mouth wide and ___.
T5.e: You yawn when you are tired or bored.

T5.q: Someone who sleeps very well and doesn't wake up easily: a heavy s___
T5.e: A heavy sleeper is difficult to wake up. The opposite is a light sleeper.

T5.q: I'm not interested in ___ to the concert.
T5.e: After a preposition (in) we use the -ing form.

T5.q: She managed ___ tickets for the festival.
T5.e: Manage + to + infinitive.

T5.q: The teacher made us ___ the song again.
T5.e: Make + person + infinitive without 'to'.

T5.q: It's worth ___ (listen) to their first album.
T5.e: It's worth + -ing form.

T5.q: This room ___ (smell) like fresh bread.
T5.e: Verbs of the senses + like + noun. With 'this room' (it) we add -s.

T5.q: My sister plays the ___ in the school orchestra.
T5.e: The violin is the instrument; a violinist is the person who plays it.

T5.q: You ___ have told Anna my secret! Now everyone knows.
T5.e: Shouldn't have + past participle to criticise something someone did in the past.

T5.q: Marco ___ have been at the party; he was in Rome that night.
T5.e: Can't have + past participle: we're sure something did not happen.

T5.q: I'd rather you ___ me the truth.
T5.e: I'd rather + another person + past simple.

T5.q: My bag isn't here. Someone ___ (must / take) it by mistake.
T5.e: Must have + past participle: we're almost sure about something in the past.

T5.q: I'll ___ you my bike if you promise to be careful.
T5.e: Lend = give something for a short time. Borrow = take something for a short time.

T5.q: The sun ___ at about six o'clock in summer.
T5.e: Rise has no object (the sun rises). Raise needs an object (raise your hand).

T5.q: You sound ___ you've got a cold.
T5.e: Sound as if / as though + clause: you sound as if you've got a cold.

T5.q: You use your t___ to taste food.
T5.e: Your tongue is in your mouth and helps you taste and speak.

T6.q: The museum ___ in 1890.
T6.e: Past simple passive: was / were + past participle.

T6.q: The suspects ___ by the police at the moment.
T6.e: Present continuous passive: am / is / are being + past participle.

T6.q: I need to ___ my eyes tested.
T6.e: Have something done: another person does it for you.

T6.q: The thieves are believed ___ through a back window.
T6.e: Be believed + perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) for a past action.

T6.q: ___ said that the mayor will resign.
T6.e: It is said that... is a formal way of reporting what people say.

T6.q: The windows ___ (clean) every Monday.
T6.e: Present simple passive: am / is / are + past participle.

T6.q: My phone was broken, so I had it ___ (repair).
T6.e: Have + object + past participle.

T6.q: A ___ steals things from people's pockets or bags in crowded places.
T6.e: A pickpocket steals from pockets and bags, usually in crowds.

T6.q: The ___ decided that she was not guilty.
T6.e: The jury is the group of people in court who decide if someone is guilty.

T6.q: He was ___ with murder.
T6.e: Charge someone with a crime. We say accused of, arrested for, blamed for.

T6.q: A person who takes someone and keeps them until money is paid: a k___
T6.e: A kidnapper takes a person and asks for money to free them.

T6.q: She ___ that she had taken the money.
T6.e: Admit (that) = say that you did something wrong.

T6.q: He ___ me of lying.
T6.e: Accuse somebody of doing something.

T6.q: My friends persuaded me ___ the competition.
T6.e: Persuade + person + to + infinitive.

T6.q: The teacher ___ that we should read more in English.
T6.e: Recommend (that) + subject + should. Told, invited and persuaded need a person after them.

T6.q: He threatened ___ (call) the police.
T6.e: Threaten + to + infinitive.

T6.q: She insisted on ___ (pay) for dinner.
T6.e: Insist on + -ing form.

T6.q: A serious newspaper, usually with long articles about politics and world news, is a ___.
T6.e: A broadsheet is a serious newspaper. A tabloid has more gossip and big photos.

T6.q: The ___ of a newspaper decides which stories are published.
T6.e: The editor is in charge of a newspaper and decides what goes in it.

T6.q: An article that is fair and doesn't take sides is the opposite of biased: u___
T6.e: Unbiased = fair, showing all sides. Biased = showing only one side.

T7.q: ___ being a millionaire, he lives in a small flat.
T7.e: Despite + -ing form or noun. Although and even though need subject + verb.

T7.q: She kept working ___ she was exhausted.
T7.e: Even though + subject + verb for a strong contrast.

T7.q: I'm learning English ___ I can study in London.
T7.e: So that + subject + verb (can/could) for purpose. In order to and to are followed by a verb.

T7.q: They whispered ___ wake the baby.
T7.e: So as not to + infinitive for a negative purpose.

T7.q: The food was delicious. The service, ___, was very slow.
T7.e: However connects two separate sentences and shows contrast.

T7.q: In ___ of the cold, we went swimming.
T7.e: In spite of + noun = despite.

T7.q: I called the shop ___ order to check the opening times.
T7.e: In order to + infinitive for purpose.

T7.q: The company is going to ___ a new product next month.
T7.e: Launch a product = introduce it to the public for the first time.

T7.q: A company with offices and factories in many countries is a ___ company.
T7.e: Multinational = working in many countries.

T7.q: Our main ___ is the shop across the road - they sell the same things.
T7.e: A competitor is a company that tries to sell the same things as you.

T7.q: To tell people about a product on TV, radio, etc. so they buy it: a___
T7.e: Advertise is the verb. The noun is advertisement (advert).

T7.q: My jeans ___ in the washing machine.
T7.e: Jeans is a plural noun, so it takes a plural verb.

T7.q: The furniture in their house ___ very modern.
T7.e: Furniture is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb.

T7.q: Can you give me ___ piece of advice?
T7.e: Advice is uncountable, but we can say 'a piece of advice'.

T7.q: The police ___ (be) at the scene within minutes yesterday.
T7.e: Police is plural, so in the past we use were.

T7.q: Which word means 'to write again'?
T7.e: The prefix re- means 'again': rewrite, redo, rebuild.

T7.q: The adjective from 'comfort' is ___.
T7.e: The suffix -able makes adjectives: comfortable, enjoyable.

T7.q: The noun from 'happy' is ___.
T7.e: The suffix -ness makes nouns from adjectives. The y changes to i: happiness.

T7.q: A person who works for a company: an ___ (employ)
T7.e: -ee is for the person who receives the action (employee). -er is the person who does it (employer).

T7.q: Not correct: ___ (correct)
T7.e: The prefix in- makes the opposite of some adjectives: correct - incorrect.

T8.q: ___ my sister nor my brother can drive.
T8.e: Neither... nor... = not one and not the other.

T8.q: You can sit on ___ side of the table; it doesn't matter.
T8.e: Either + singular noun = one or the other of two.

T8.q: ___ the students passed the exam. The teacher was very happy.
T8.e: All + the + plural noun. Every and each are used with a singular noun without 'the'.

T8.q: I spent ___ day at the beach.
T8.e: The whole + singular noun = all of it: the whole day.

T8.q: There's ___ time left. We have to hurry!
T8.e: Hardly any = almost no. We don't say 'no any' or 'hardly no'.

T8.q: B___ of my grandparents live in Bagheria.
T8.e: Both = the two of them. It takes a plural verb.

T8.q: We had no money, so we couldn't buy a___ tickets.
T8.e: We use any in negative sentences: couldn't buy any.

T8.q: The new medicine has to be ___ on volunteers before it's sold.
T8.e: Test = try something to see if it works and is safe.

T8.q: A person who studies chemistry is a ___.
T8.e: A chemist is a scientist who studies chemistry. A chemical is a substance.

T8.q: Galileo made an important ___ about the moons of Jupiter.
T8.e: We make a discovery when we find something that already existed. Research is uncountable, so we can't say 'a research'.

T8.q: To show that something is true: p___
T8.e: Prove = show that something is true, using evidence.

T8.q: ___ Sicily is the largest island in ___ Mediterranean.
T8.e: No article with most islands (Sicily). We use 'the' with seas (the Mediterranean).

T8.q: I love ___ music, especially jazz.
T8.e: No article when we talk about things in general: I love music.

T8.q: Can you close ___ door, please? It's cold.
T8.e: We use 'the' when both people know which one we mean.

T8.q: ___ Thames flows through London.
T8.e: We use 'the' with the names of rivers: the Thames, the Nile.

T8.q: She's ___ best player in the team.
T8.e: We use 'the' with superlatives: the best.

T8.q: My uncle works as ___ architect.
T8.e: We use a / an with jobs. 'An' before a vowel sound: an architect.

T8.q: The rules here are black and ___.
T8.e: Black and white = very clear, with no doubt.

T8.q: Take your time, there's no need to rush. Slow and ___ wins the race.
T8.e: Slow and steady is a word pair: doing something carefully and regularly.

T8.q: We've tried again and a___, but we still can't open this door.
T8.e: Again and again = many times.
